analysis.one_liner: Raises the salary cutoff below which salaried workers must get overtime pay, updated yearly.
analysis.headline: A bill restoring overtime pay to millions of salaried workers has sat in a Senate committee since May 2026 with 28 cosponsors and no action.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal overtime rules let employers skip overtime pay for salaried 'executive, administrative, and professional' workers, no matter how little they earn. This bill would set a minimum salary for that exemption: $45,000 at first, rising on a fixed schedule to $75,000 by 2029, then automatically tracking the 55th percentile of national salaried earnings each year. It would also tighten the duties test so salaried managers who spend most of their time on ordinary work cannot be classified as exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning between roughly $35,000 and $75,000 who are currently classified as exempt and work more than 40 hours a week. Under the bill, employers would owe them time-and-a-half for hours over 40, or would have to raise their salaries above the threshold to keep them exempt. Workers whose job duties are mostly routine rather than managerial would gain protection even at higher salaries.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a hard salary floor for the overtime exemption, starting at $45,000 and stepping up to $55,000, $65,000, and $75,000 in successive years; below that line, salaried workers must be paid time-and-a-half for hours over 40.

From 2030, the threshold automatically updates each year to the 55th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers nationally, so future rule changes by a different administration cannot quietly erode it, and updates bypass ordinary notice-and-comment rulemaking.

Narrows the 'nonexempt duties' allowance for retail and service workers so that exempt employees must spend at least 80 percent of their time on genuinely executive or administrative work, limiting the common practice of salarying low-level managers while they perform ordinary hourly tasks.
Requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish quarterly weekly-earnings data by census region, making the threshold's basis publicly verifiable.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with salaried employees under the threshold — restaurants, retail chains, health care providers, nonprofits, and small businesses — would owe overtime or higher salaries for workers between roughly $45,000 and $75,000 who work long hours. Some employers would cut hours or restructure jobs to avoid the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers of modestly paid salaried workers

drawbacks.text: Employers facing higher overtime bills for salaried staff between $45,000 and $75,000 may respond by cutting hours, converting salaried roles to hourly ones, or raising salaries only for the few workers just under the line — outcomes that reduce take-home pay for some of the workers the bill aims to help.

A national 55th-percentile threshold applies the same dollar figure everywhere; in lower-wage regions it could sweep in supervisory and professional roles that local labor markets already treat as salaried, and the automatic annual updates skip notice-and-comment rulemaking, giving the Department of Labor limited flexibility to adjust for regional or economic conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the target group — salaried workers in the $45,000-$75,000 band who routinely work over 40 hours — the gain is direct: overtime pay or a raise. The costs fall on employers, especially in low-margin industries and lower-wage regions, and some of those costs can shift back onto workers through reduced hours or reclassification. The design is fairly aggressive (a national percentile threshold with automatic updates and little regulatory flexibility), which is a real trade-off, not just a talking point, but the core mechanism — requiring overtime below a defined salary — is the same one federal law has applied through regulation for decades.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill in the Senate on May 18, 2026.
It was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; the action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action since.
It has 28 cosponsors, all of them Senate Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of salaried workers under the eventual thresholds — restaurants, retail, health care, and other businesses that rely on salaried managers working long hours without overtime — are better off because the bill has not advanced. Workers in that pay band are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of modestly paid salaried managers

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Restoring Overtime Pay Act of 2026 and recruited 28 Senate Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 28 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Chuck Schumer, Elizabeth Warren, Tammy Baldwin, and Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, controls whether it gets a hearing or markup; no committee action has occurred since the bill was referred in May 2026.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 55 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support needed to advance.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats or the chamber's Independents; none of the 55 Senate Republicans support it, and Republicans control both the Senate and the committee of referral.

industries.industry: Restaurants and retail (employers of salaried store and restaurant managers)
industries.note: These industries rely heavily on salaring low- and mid-paid managers who work long hours without overtime. A $45,000-$75,000 threshold forces them to pay overtime or raise salaries, and the tightened duties test targets exactly the 'working manager' classification they use. Their savings from the current system come at the direct expense of workers' unpaid overtime hours.

industries.industry: Health care providers and social services
industries.note: Large employers of salaried supervisors and coordinators in the $45,000-$75,000 band, including nonprofit providers, would face new overtime obligations for staff who work long shifts.
Organizations with tight budgets and few salaried staff would bear the same new overtime costs as large firms, without the staffing flexibility of bigger employers.

Workers just above the threshold gain overtime rights; some could see hours cut or roles converted to hourly as employers adjust, a trade-off the bill's supporters acknowledge implicitly by phasing the threshold in over four years.

analysis.trajectory: With 28 of 45 Senate Democrats signed on but no Republican support, a Republican-controlled Senate, and no movement in the HELP Committee since referral in May 2026, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in this Congress — the standard path for a party-line labor bill in the minority's first act of business.
